labels.heading: Letter to R. M. Hughes from Chin-Wu Huang - Antioch College and Ford
labels.text: Being in the formative years of our lives, for most, college is a cherished time, especially upon reflection, such was the case for Chin-Wu Huang. After leaving Miami, Huang would continue his studies at Antioch College, pursuing an accounting route in the auto manufacturing industry. In his letter to President Hughes, Huang expresses not only his longing for going back to Miami, but gives several updates to his life. In addition to studying at Antioch College, Huang would find a temporary job at Ford in Highland Parks, Michigan. Huang uses this job and his experiences in higher education to reflect on the state of industry practices in China, hoping that the young republic will eventually grow to American standards.

labels.heading: Letter to President Hahne from H. H. Chang - Funding for Kwang Hua University
labels.text: The year before H. H. Chang sent this letter to President Hahne, Chang had given a lecture series in Oxford regarding international studies on the invitation of President Hahne. After seeing a newspaper segment on President Hahne being celebrated at a Miami University Alumni Chapter in New York City in early 1947, Chang reached back out to Hahne in this letter regarding his objective in the States. Chang was looking for funding opportunities for Kwang Hua University of which he was a professor and an administrator. He expressed to the worldly Hahne that to fund such a university was critical for China in this transformative period. Hahne would provide not only contacts for this endeavor but write, “Be assured that as a sister institution, Miami University is very deeply interested in the success of the University of Shanghai, and personally my best wishes are for the attainment of effective results in a nation we have grown to respect and love.”

labels.heading: Letter to H. H. Chang from President Hahne - Invite to Lecture in Oxford
labels.text: In a confusing post World War Two world, where the dynamics of world order have been fundamentally changed, perhaps no one better could speak on it than one of the foremost authorities in international studies and global diplomacy, Dr. H. H. Chang. The Johns Hopkins and Harvard grad, Chang had produced brilliant work throughout his career, including a particularly engaging lecture on the relations between the U.S., China and Russia. Hahne attended the original lecture and knew that it would be invaluable for Miami students.

labels.heading: Letter to R. M. Hughes from C. H. Chuang - Living Situation and Updates
labels.text: This letter reveals several stories of not only Chuang’s time at Miami, but of several other Chinese classmates, most of whom also attended Tsing Hua College prior to Miami. Many of the Chinese alumni who had attended Miami would later take up important positions in the burgeoning China, such as Leo Shen, class of 1919. Shen would go on to study at Chicago and Columbia to then return as a middle school principal in China.

labels.heading: Letter to C. H. Chuang from R. M. Hughes - Tsing Hua Grading Issues
labels.text: While Tsing Hua College evidently prepared many high achieving Chinese Miami alumni, the ability to assess their readiness and knowledge upon their admission to Miami was inconsistent. Universities across the country, from Stanford to Colorado College, all encountered the issue of how to accurately place Tsing Hua students. If students were placed as seniors, their academic performance would suffer from the excessive difficulty. If they were placed as freshmen, it would be insulting to the Tsing Hua curriculum. Hughes would emphasize that above all, maintaining a healthy number of Chinese students was critical to the diplomacy of China and the U.S.
